notes: Van Hoogstraten case management; directions upheld and costs appeal refused.

enrichment.short_title: Raja v Van Hoogstraten: case management after murder-related civil claims
key_facts: Mohammed Raja was murdered in 1999; Nicholas Van Hoogstraten was acquitted on appeal after an earlier manslaughter conviction.
Family members brought Queen's Bench actions for damages and a Chancery action over property and conspiracy, later amended to allege abuse of process.
After a Court of Appeal order reversing Peter Smith J's strike-out, Lightman J at a case management conference set a trial timetable for all four actions, including transfer of the QB claims.
Van Hoogstraten, acting in person after dismissing his lawyers, applied to discharge the order, refused permission to appeal costs, and threatened not to comply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application to discharge case management directions and for permission to appeal a costs order after a case management conference.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; case management directions upheld, permission to appeal the costs order refused, and Van Hoogstraten ordered to abide by the agreed timetable including trial on 14 November 2005.
enrichment.ratio: A litigant in person cannot veto court case management directions agreed by counsel and approved by the judge; gratuitous abuse of the judiciary is unacceptable and may invite sanctions.
legal_issues: Whether counsel had authority to agree case management directions at the hearing
Whether the defendant could refuse to comply without consent
Whether permission to appeal the costs order should be granted
Whether freezing orders precluded funding the litigation

confidence.notes: Interlocutory procedural ruling with clear final orders on the applications before the court.

notes: Rent review trigger notice and counter-notice split decision; Mannai/Nunes tests applied.

enrichment.short_title: Lancecrest v Asiwaju: late rent review notice and valid counter-notice
key_facts: Lancecrest acquired the reversion to a 12-year retail lease with a rent review every four years and served a trigger notice 54 weeks after the first review date proposing £30,000.
Dr Asiwaju replied within two months disputing the notice and refusing to enter arbitration, but also challenging the landlord's right to review at all.
An independent surveyor fixed the new basic rent at £28,000 after the tenant made no submissions.
The county court held the late trigger notice valid but the tenant's letter was not a valid counter-notice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Bow County Court on construction of rent review and counter-notice clauses.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on the validity of the late trigger notice and allowed on counter-notice validity; rent from 5 February 2001 fixed at £28,000 per annum.
enrichment.ratio: Under United Scientific Holdings time is not of the essence for a landlord's rent review notice unless made so by the tenant; a tenant's reply can be a valid counter-notice if it clearly informs the landlord he does not accept the proposed rent, applying Mannai and Nunes principles.
legal_issues: Whether time was of the essence for service of the landlord's trigger notice
Whether a late trigger notice under clause 5.1(b) was effective
Whether the tenant's letter constituted a valid counter-notice under clause 5.1(c)
Whether the recipient landlord's reaction is relevant to notice validity
linked_authorities: United Scientific Holdings Ltd v Burnley Borough Council [1978] AC 904
Mannai Investment Co Ltd v Eagle Star Life Assurance Co Ltd [1997] AC 749
Nunes v Davies Laing & Dick Ltd (1985) 51 P&CR 310

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate reasoning on both issues with a clear split decision and final rent figure.

notes: T&N asbestos administration; reinsurers' claims-handling rights and cost reimbursement upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Freakley v Centre Re: T&N asbestos claims handling in administration
key_facts: T&N Limited entered administration in October 2001 amid massive UK and US asbestos personal injury claims after Federal-Mogul's Chapter 11 filing.
Curzon insured T&N under a £500 million asbestos liability policy with a £690 million retention, reinsured by Centre Re and others.
Disputes arose whether reinsurers or administrators should handle asbestos claims and who bore claims-handling costs.
Blackburne J held reinsurers entitled to handle claims and to reimbursement from T&N, but rejected treating reimbursement as an administration expense.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from Blackburne J's order resolving insurance and administration issues in T&N's administration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed on the first group of issues; reinsurers' entitlement to handle claims and to reimbursement upheld, without priority as an administration expense.
enrichment.ratio: On the true construction of the asbestos liability policy and reinsurance agreement, administration triggered reinsurers' rights to handle asbestos claims and to reimbursement of claims-handling costs as ultimate net loss, but not automatic treatment as an administration expense.
legal_issues: Who was entitled to handle asbestos claims after the administration order
Whether reinsurers must bear or could recover claims-handling costs
Whether reimbursement ranked as an expense of the administration
Construction of the asbestos liability policy and reinsurance agreement

confidence.notes: Complex multi-issue judgment but principal dispositions on the first issue group are clearly stated.

notes: M27 subcontract trial; oral contract with Hanson found on 15 October 2001 meeting.

enrichment.short_title: Davidson v Hanson: identity of subcontractor on M27 motorway works
key_facts: Mr Davidson, a slip-form drainage specialist, carried out works on the M27 Junctions 2-4 carriageway renewal for Hanson and Stenoak joint venture.
Hanson contended Davidson contracted with Stenoak or Associated Asphalt Ltd on 15 October 2001; Davidson said he orally contracted with Hanson personnel at Chipping Sodbury.
Stenoak became insolvent in June 2002; Hanson terminated the joint venture and disputed liability for £209,077.74 agreed subject to liability.
Evidence centred on meetings on 19/28 September and 15 October 2001 and subsequent correspondence addressed to Hanson.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial on whether the subcontract was with Hanson or Stenoak/AAL.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Davidson; he entered into a contract with Hanson on 15 October 2001 and is entitled to the agreed sum of £209,077.74.
enrichment.ratio: Where Hanson personnel negotiated and concluded terms without telling the subcontractor he was contracting with Stenoak/AAL, and post-contract conduct consistently treated Hanson as the contracting party, an oral contract with Hanson was formed on acceptance of the offer at the 15 October meeting.
legal_issues: Whether the 15 October 2001 meeting created a contract and with whom
Whether an earlier September meeting occurred and its significance
Effect of unsigned Stenoak sub-contract documents and payments by AAL
Whether Hanson personnel acted as agents for Stenoak

confidence.notes: Fact-intensive trial with a clear finding on contractual identity and undisputed quantum.

notes: Fraudulent insurance claims rule; whole claim forfeited including pre-fraud payments.

enrichment.short_title: AXA v Gottlieb: scope of the fraudulent insurance claims rule
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Gottlieb made four buildings insurance claims under an Axa policy in 1993-94, including dry rot and escape of water.
Mrs Gottlieb was found to have fraudulently claimed alternative accommodation via builder Mr Galvin from late September 1999 and to have submitted a forged electrician's invoice in June 2000.
The judge held Axa could recover all payments on the fraudulent claims (1) and (2) but not on unrelated claims (3) and (4).
Late application to appeal the fraud findings was refused; the parties appealed and cross-appealed on the measure of recovery.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal on application of the common law rule relating to fraudulent insurance claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; insurers may recover interim payments made before fraud on the same claim because the whole claim is forfeited.
enrichment.ratio: The common law rule on fraudulent insurance claims forfeits the entire claim to which the fraud relates, so prior payments on genuine loss on that claim fail for want of consideration and are recoverable, distinct from s.17 avoidance or general repudiation principles.
legal_issues: Whether the fraudulent claims rule applies retrospectively to pre-fraud payments on the same claim
Whether unrelated settled claims are recoverable after fraud on another claim
Whether Mihalis Angelos requires events to be predestined at the date of repudiation
Whether an extension of time to appeal fraud findings should be granted
linked_authorities: Manifest Shipping Co Ltd v Uni-Polaris Ins Co (The Star Sea) [2001] UKHL 1
Maredelanto Compania Naviera SA v Bergbau-Handel GmbH (The Mihalis Angelos) [1971] 1 QB 164

confidence.notes: Authoritative Court of Appeal analysis with clear ratio on the central insurance law issue.

notes: Homelessness possession appeal allowed; Article 8 and out-of-time review rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Tower Hamlets v Begum: homelessness duty and possession after refused offer
key_facts: Tower Hamlets accepted Mrs Begum as unintentionally homeless with priority need and placed her in temporary accommodation at Allonby House with no security of tenure.
She refused a permanent offer at Brimsdown House; the council's 25 January 2002 letter did not satisfy section 193(7)(b) notification requirements.
By May 2002 the council decided its section 193 duty had ended and began possession proceedings; the county court dismissed the claim relying on Article 8.
Begum neither requested a section 202 review nor appealed under section 204 within the statutory time limits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from possession proceedings where the tenant resisted on the basis the council remained under a homelessness duty.
enrichment.outcome: Council's appeal allowed; order for possession to be made, as the tenant could not collaterally challenge the homelessness decision long out of time.
enrichment.ratio: Where Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 provides review and appeal procedures with strict time limits, a tenant cannot resist possession by relitigating the section 193 duty in possession proceedings or by late judicial review; Article 8 rarely assists in such cases after Qazi.
legal_issues: Whether the 25 January 2002 letter satisfied section 193(7)(b)
Whether the council remained under a duty to accommodate the tenant
Whether Article 8 could defeat the possession claim
Whether a late section 204 appeal or judicial review could be entertained
linked_authorities: London Borough of Harrow v Qazi [2004] 1 AC 983
Sheffield City Council v Smart [2002] HLR 639

confidence.notes: Comprehensive procedural and statutory analysis with a clear appellate disposition.

notes: Munby J guidance on family court and SENDIST jurisdiction overlap in care cases.

enrichment.short_title: X County Council v DW: family court and SENDIST in care proceedings
key_facts: Care proceedings concerned a 10-year-old boy with autistic spectrum disorder; an interim care order was made in favour of X County Council.
The local education authority issued a statement of special educational needs naming a maintained special school, consistent with the approved interim care plan.
The issue was what would happen if parents appealed to SENDIST and the tribunal amended the statement in conflict with the care plan.
Munby J gave guidance on the separate but related functions of the family court and SENDIST.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial guidance in ongoing care proceedings on the interaction between family court welfare jurisdiction and SENDIST appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Guidance given: the family court and SENDIST perform separate functions; neither can dictate to the other, though each must take account of the other's orders, and parents may appeal to SENDIST even where the local authority holds parental responsibility.
enrichment.ratio: School placement is an aspect of parental responsibility exercisable by the local authority under a care order, but parents (including a corporate parent) retain section 326 appeal rights; SENDIST and the family court apply different statutory tests and any conflict is resolved by public law principles, not family law alone.
legal_issues: Respective jurisdiction of the family court and SENDIST
Whether a local authority with a care order can appeal as a parent under section 326
Whether the family court can compel a school or education authority to admit a child
Consequences if SENDIST and the family court reach different conclusions on placement
linked_authorities: Fairpo v Humberside County Council [1997] ELR 12
A v A Health Authority, In re J (A Child) [2002] EWHC 18 (Fam/Admin)
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex p T [1995] 1 FLR 293

confidence.notes: Clear principled guidance from a leading authority though not disposing of the underlying care proceedings.

notes: Summary judgment reversed; disputed oral compromise on investment advisory termination.

enrichment.short_title: Merchantbridge v Safron GP: disputed oral compromise on advisory contract
key_facts: Safron Advisors UK Ltd provided investment advice to Safron General Partner I Ltd under a January 2001 agreement paying $1,110,000 for 2001.
After a June 2001 board decision to wind down the Safron Group, SGP1 terminated the agreement; a meeting on 22 June 2001 produced unsigned minutes.
Morison J granted summary judgment holding an oral compromise forbade wrongful-termination proceedings in exchange for payment of creditors and wind-down costs.
Mr Al-Rahim disputed any such oral agreement and later proposed a mutual release conditional on five specified matters in a 10 July memorandum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment under CPR Part 24 on whether an oral compromise barred the wrongful termination claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; disputed oral agreement unsuitable for summary determination and alternative unpleaded agreement could not support summary judgment.
enrichment.ratio: Summary judgment is inappropriate where the existence of a disputed oral compromise is central; a respondent's notice relying on a different unpleaded agreement formed by a later memorandum cannot sustain Part 24 judgment.
legal_issues: Whether parties orally agreed on 22 June 2001 not to sue for wrongful termination
Whether the 10 July 2001 memorandum constituted a separate binding compromise
Whether Part 24 summary judgment was available on disputed oral evidence
Whether a respondent's notice can introduce an unpleaded agreement

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning clearly reverses summary judgment though factual compromise issues remain for trial.

notes: Golden Victory damages; Gulf War war clause limited recoverable charter hire loss.

enrichment.short_title: Golden Victory: charterparty damages and subsequent war cancellation
key_facts: NYKK repudiated a seven-year charter of the Golden Victory in December 2001 with about four years remaining.
The charter contained a war clause allowing cancellation if war broke out between listed countries including the UK, Iraq and the USA.
The second Gulf War in March 2003 was held a qualifying war and the arbitrator found NYKK would have cancelled.
GSC claimed damages as charter rate less market rate for the full balance; NYKK argued damages ended when the war clause would have been invoked.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court appeal under section 69 of the Arbitration Act 1996 on assessment of damages for repudiatory breach of a time charter.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; damages for the repudiation were temporally limited to the period before the March 2003 war that would have triggered cancellation.
enrichment.ratio: Where a charter would inevitably have been cancelled under a war clause before expiry, damages for wrongful repudiation are not assessed for the full charter period at market rate less contract rate; subsequent events showing the charter would not have run its course may be taken into account despite an available market at breach.
legal_issues: Whether damages are fixed once and for all at repudiation where there is an available market
Whether subsequent Gulf War events limit recoverable hire loss
Construction of the charter war cancellation clause
Application of The Mihalis Angelos and The Seaflower
linked_authorities: Maredelanto Compania Naviera SA v Bergbau-Handel GmbH (The Mihalis Angelos) [1971] 1 QB 164
Koch Marine Inc v D'Amica Societa di Navigazione (The Elena d'Amico) [1980] 1 Lloyd's Rep 75
B.S.&N. Ltd v Micado Shipping Ltd (The Seaflower) [2000] 2 Lloyd's Rep 37

notes: Reinstatement compensation; section 117(3) may revisit pre-reinstatement loss.

enrichment.short_title: Awotona v South Tyneside: compensation after failed reinstatement order
key_facts: Dr Awotona, a consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist, was unfairly dismissed and racially victimised by South Tyneside Healthcare NHS Trust.
The employment tribunal ordered reinstatement by 1 April 2003 and specified £148,704 net under section 114(2)(a) for the pre-reinstatement period.
The Trust failed to reinstate; the tribunal initially refused to reopen evidence of lost family planning income but later allowed it under section 117(2).
The EAT held section 117(3) compensation could not revisit losses already covered by the section 114(2) award.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on construction of sections 114 and 117 when reinstatement is not complied with.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; on non-compliance with reinstatement, compensatory award under section 117(3)(a) is calculated afresh under sections 118-127 and may reconsider pre-reinstatement loss, while the section 114(2) amount still affects the section 124 statutory cap.
enrichment.ratio: Section 114(2) and section 117(3)(a) perform different exercises; failure to reinstate triggers a fresh just-and-equitable compensatory assessment that may revisit earlier loss, though the section 114(2) figure remains for the limited purpose of calculating whether the section 124 cap may be exceeded.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal could reopen evidence excluded at an earlier remedies hearing
Whether section 117(3) precludes reconsideration of pre-reinstatement loss already specified under section 114(2)
The role of section 124(4) when reinstatement fails
Distinction between section 114 reinstatement arithmetic and section 123 compensatory assessment
